L01.why: Conditional perfect needs a counterfactual frame the other tenses do not, but such a frame could exist.

L02.why: All four auxiliaries can each fit some frame; 'did' is least likely if a participle follows.

L03.why: Present progressive is the odd tense out, but a present-time context could license it.

L04.why: No punctuation likely fuses two clauses, though 'frame three' could be a single phrase.

L05.why: Active 'would have damped out' needs an object/agent arrangement the passive forms avoid, but it can work.

L06.why: Plural 'have given' is the odd agreement form, but a plural subject could license it.

L07.why: The semicolon requires an independent clause on both sides, which the comma versions do not.

L08.why: A single comma between compound subject and verb is usually wrong, but an earlier opening comma could pair with it.

L09.why: 'However' between commas often produces a comma splice, though it can be grammatical in some frames.

L10.why: All four verb forms can fit some subject and time frame.

L11.why: Comma between subject and verb is wrong unless paired with an earlier comma.

L12.why: 'stocks ... stays' mixes forms, but 'stocks' could be a verb in a relative clause with a singular subject.

L13.why: Past perfect needs an earlier past reference point, but one could exist.

L14.why: No punctuation likely fuses two clauses, though an introductory phrase could run on without a comma.

L15.why: 'that's' as a relative pronoun is nonstandard, but it can be read as 'that is'.

L16.why: Present perfect is the odd tense among past-perfect options, but a present frame could license it.

L17.why: Past perfect active is the odd form, but an earlier reference point could license it.

L18.why: All four forms fit some subject and tense frame.

L19.why: Expletive 'it was found' cannot be modified by a leading participial phrase, which the sentence likely has, but none is guaranteed.

L20.why: The comma after 'trains' separates subject from verb with no opening comma between them to pair with.

L21.why: A semicolon before a dependent 'that' clause is usually wrong, though 'That the...' could begin an independent clause.

L22.why: A semicolon before 'that' is usually wrong, though 'That ...' could start an independent clause.

L23.why: Active singular 'seals' is the odd voice-number combo, but a singular agent subject could license it.

L24.why: 'those of a seal's' is a redundant double possessive that is almost never right in a comparison.

L25.why: Missing the closing parenthesis the other options supply, though the hidden text may have no parenthesis.

L26.why: Past 'were' breaks the present tense of the other three, but a past frame could license it.

L27.why: 'and because' loses the contrast the 'but' options imply, but a non-contrastive frame could license it.

L28.why: It reverses the logical order (discovering before climbing), though it is grammatical.

L29.why: A colon between a verb and its object is never correct; likewise a colon splitting 'diversity' from 'of corals'.

L30.why: No punctuation may run a modifier into the clause, but it could be a single prepositional phrase.

L31.why: If a leading modifier describes Marcus, a pier subject dangles, but no modifier is guaranteed.

L32.why: 'that one anticipates' is the least parallel form, but some frames take a that-clause.

L33.why: Expletive construction likely dangles a leading modifier, but none is guaranteed.

L34.why: 'result differing' without a comma is usually a fragment, but an absolute or noun-modifier reading is possible.

L35.why: 'is modeling' is the odd progressive, but a present-progressive frame could license it.

L36.why: Nominalized subject usually leaves the clause verbless or dangles a modifier, but a following verb could complete it.

L37.why: Past progressive is the odd tense, but a past frame could license it.

L38.why: All four forms can fit some subject and tense.

L39.why: No punctuation runs the clauses together, though the clause could continue grammatically.

L40.why: Comma after 'but' looks wrong, though 'but, because X, Y' is valid when the clause is interrupted.
